Figure 5:  Tape layer stackup for original tape design.  Middle three layers (bolded in red) was a commercially available double-sided copper substrate product; copper layers were subsequently etched to create copper crosshatch shield layer and copper signal/power trace layer.  Note the copper layers are not at the neutral bending axis (middle) of the tape which causes increased strain and fatigue on the copper during bending.

 

The initial CLARREO Pathfinder HPS flex harness design was derived from the TSIS-1 flex harness design in consideration of the prior life test for TSIS-1.  The minimum flexural life needed for the CLARREO Pathfinder harnesses was 15,000 cycles, equivalent to 1x mission life.  A life test to 2x mission life (30,000 cycles) was planned in the project schedule but was delayed in execution due to multiple factors, including necessary maturation of the flex harness design, limited number of vendors with the capability to fabricate the harnesses, lengthy production schedules, and COVID-19.  A life test of the HPS azimuth flex harness life test unit was initiated in summer 2020 after the project’s Critical Design Review and an extended facility shutdown due to COVID-19.  Figure 6 shows a photograph of the life test fixture with test harness installed.  Copper traces within the life test harness began exhibiting inconsistent and high resistance values starting at approximately 2000 cycles, indicating signs of early failure.  Under continued flexing additional copper traces exhibited high resistance/open circuit.  The life test was deemed a test failure and stopped at 20,000 cycles, at which time nearly all coppr traces exhibited signs of failure.

​The CLARREO Pathfinder project initiated an investigation into the HPS flex harness life test failure mechanism(s) and harness design.  Technical assistance was sought from the NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) who contributed personnel with expertise that greatly assisted in the investigation.  The investigation lasted approximately five months concluding in January 2021.  Multiple non-destructive evaluation (NDE), destructive physical analysis (DPA), and analytical techniques were used to identify and characterize mechanisms contributing to the failure of copper traces within the flex harness.  The root cause of the copper trace failures was fatigue cracking of the copper signal traces predominantly in locations that were overlapped by the crosshatch copper traces within the shield layer.  A factor contributing to the copper trace failures was that each flex tape within the harness was a “double-sided” layup configuration where the copper signal trace layer was located away from the neutral bending axis of the tape, causing increased mechanical strain and fatigue on the traces during flexing.

 

The investigation produced multiple recommendations for a redesigned flex harness and life testing methodology.  Key recommendations for redesign were:

  1. Use single-sided copper ribbons with the copper as close as possible to the neutral plane
  2. Use wider copper traces than the original design. Consider 30 mils. Use modeling to validate if ½ oz copper is the best option for meeting the life test requirement for the flex ribbon harness.
  3. Add IPC 2223 dynamic flex requirements to design requirements (minimum flex cycles per IPC test method
  4. Add a second vendor source
  5. Assess CLARREO on-orbit operational requirements to determine the life test parameters
  6. Include temperature extremes in the life test and if possible vacuum conditions.

Many of the NESC’s recommendations were adopted and incorporated into the redesigned HPS azimuth and elevation flex harnesses and life testing plan.  A redesigned azimuth flex harness successfully passed a 4X life test (60,000 cycles) in December 2021.  Test cycles were completed at ambient, hot operational, and cold operational temperatures at atmospheric pressure (not vacuum).  Key design aspects for the redesigned flex tapes comprising the harnesses were:

  • Single-sided flex tape layup construction with copper trace layer located in the center of the tape, at the neutral bending axis, as shown in Figure 7.
  • Elimination of crosshatch copper shield layer within the tapes.  A separate tape consisting of only the copper crosshatch pattern was added to the harness for shielding purposes.
  • Single-sided copper clad polyimide substrate.  Consists of 2-mil Kapton coverlay and 0.7 mil (e.g. ½ oz.) copper layer
  • ½-oz. Rolled Highly Annealed Copper, minimum 30 mil trace width
  • Kapton® coverlay 1 mil thick, 1 mil acrylic coverlay adhesive
  • No part identification markings (i.e., silk-screened lettering) in the flexing portion of the tape (no such markings existed in the flexing portion of the tape in the original design, but restated here due to importance)

lesson: Dynamically flexed flex tapes and/or harnesses should be considered an engineering development activity in project formulation, particularly for tapes/harnesses that will experience high cycle fatigue with cycle counts ≥ 500.  Therefore, projects should plan to develop test coupons and prototypes and conduct testing at representative strain levels and life cycle counts early in the project, ideally Phase B.  These early tests can help to evaluate the design principles, the selected material system, and vendor fabrication capabilities.  Identifying and using more than one vendor provides additional options.
recommendation:
Some specific flex-tape recommendations for dynamically flexed tapes include:

  • Keep the copper traces as close to the neutral bending axis as possible.
    • Whenever possible, use single-sided flex layup construction (i.e., Kapton – Copper – Kapton) with the copper trace layer located at the neutral bending axis of the tape.  
    • Ensure there is no part identification markings (e.g., silk-screened lettering) in the flexing region of the tape/harness.  The presence of silk-screened lettering can locally skew the location of the neutral bending axis, and the edges of the silk-screen lettering can act as stress concentrators that could lead to localized copper trace failures.  
    • If multi-layer “double-sided” flex tape layups must be used, avoid having copper traces overlap each other.  This results in an “I-beam” effect that increases mechanical strain on the traces which may cause copper trace fracture (see Figure 7-11 in Fjelstad, J., Flexible Circuit Technology, 4th Edition).  
  • High-purity, rolled, annealed copper is generally preferred for high-cycle flexural applications.  If rolled annealed copper is selected, be aware that rolled annealed copper typically exhibits anisotropy in the copper grain structure due to the rolling process. This anisotropy is often identified using the convention of “Machine” vs. “Cross-Machine” directions, referring to the direction in which the copper was rolled in the rolling machine.  For high cycle dynamic flexing applications rolled annealed copper should be oriented such that the “Machine” direction runs parallel to the copper traces. 
  • Flex tapes/harness designs configured in a “clock spring” configuration may be preferable to tapes/harnesses in an “Omega” configuration as the clock spring design may offer lower mechanical strain on the copper traces.  
  • When life testing, ensure the test is representative of the in-service conditions expected including range and rate of motion as well as environmental conditions.  NASA-STD-5001B specifies a service life factor of 4.0 be applied for fatigue life assessments.  For very-high-cycle applications that would make life testing prohibitively long in duration, fatigue cycle tests of coupons in a flexural testing machine (see IPC-TM-650 Section 2.4.3.1) can be used to construct a Manson-Coffin plot to evaluate predicted fatigue life.
  • When a copper trace failure occurs as indicated by an increase in resistance or open circuit, thermographic imaging of the traces with current flowing through them has been demonstrated to be an effective method for quickly diagnosing the approximate location of the break.  Additional diagnostic methods that have been used successfully are XRay/Computed Tomography (CT) imaging and Time Domain Reflectometry.

title: Magnetospheric Multiscale Mission (MMS) Laser Hole Problem in JANS Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT)
driving_event: During thermal vacuum testing late in integration and testing ( I&T), after hundreds of hours of testing involving the part, a JANS 2N2222 failed due to corrosion internal to the part.  Failure analysis indicated an aggressive solvent had entered the part through a hole created by an errant laser etching process.  The part had been leak tested, but the test was ineffective.   The laser-etched hole permitted corrosive solvents to enter the part and get trapped inside, causing corrosion.  Variants of the laser etching problem had existed for over 10 years, but this was never addressed because the parts had passed all of the necessary testing for JANS.
lesson:
• The reliance on hermetic parts can drive up both technical and programmatic risk by (1) trapping contaminants in the parts during the manufacturing process, (2) allowing contaminants to enter the parts for those that are on the fine edge of being hermetic, and (3) providing false confidence that the use of such parts provides substantial protection against part failure due to corrosion.
  • The sample size for residual gas analysis (RGA)  testing under MIL-PRF-19500 only provides a top-level indicator that parts in the lot are free from significant elevated moisture or contaminants.
  • The use of JANS parts is neither necessary or sufficient for assuring integrity or reliability of parts through I&T.
recommendation: Recognize that parts intended to be hermetic are subject to screening and destructive physical analysis (DPA) processes that allow some forms of escapes that permit corrosive elements to enter the cavity, albeit at low likelihood.

title: Copper Tube Pinch Failure
driving_event: A copper tube was pinched as a test for the Mass Spectrometer observing lunar operations (MSolo) Calibration Gas System (CGS). A CT scan revealed that a pinch that was seemingly acceptable later separated to form a leak path.
lesson:
The pinch was initially visually inspected and helium leak checked and no visual anomalies or leaks were detected. After a CT scan revealed that the seemingly acceptable pinch  separated after the helium leak check to form a leak path, an investigation was started to try to form an empirical method for verifying that a pinch has cold welded correctly. The team first turned to industry experts on copper tube pinching. While they offered a plethora of tips and tricks to try to get the best pinch possible, they were not able to provide an empirical method to ensure that a flight pinch is sealed correctly. The MSolo team then performed CT scans and inverted metallography on several copper tube pinches in an attempt to find measurements on the pinch cross-section that could be taken to distinguish a “good” pinch from a “bad” one. The results were documented, but they varied and were not useful for definitively deeming a pinch to be acceptable or not. The CT scans and inverted metallography did, however, provide insight into the shape of the pinch. A pinch with a nominal shape is more likely to have cold welded correctly. This was useful in conjunction with how the operator “felt” the pinch went. The pinch tool operator pinched several dozen practice samples and could tell from experience when a pinch didn't feel right. When some of those samples were CT scanned, the scan showed an off-nominal shape. An off-nominal shape does not guarantee that the pinch did not cold weld but when conducting our final flight pinch, we re-pinched to increase the chances of flying a successful pinch with a nominal shape.

The team also took into account some lessons learned from copper tube pinch failures for spaceflight applications in the past. The pinch point is delicate and can potentially leak if impacted. These lessons learned urged those using pinched copper tubes in spaceflight applications to protect the pinch point of the copper tube during transit and in-flight, if possible.
recommendation:
• Have pinch tool operator perform several practice pinches until he/she has an intuitive feel for the pinch tool kickback that occurs for a quotgoodquot pinch versus a quotbadquot pinch.
  • Perform CT scans and/or inverted metallography to observe the shape of the pinch.
  • Use some means of protection for the pinch point during transit and in-flight, if possible.

title: Shuttle Orbiter Airlock Hatch Failure Caused By Loose Screw On STS-80 Prevented Two Planned Mission EVAs
driving_event:
During the Space Shuttle STS-80 mission, the two planned Extravehicular Activities (EVA) were scrubbed when the astronauts discovered that the outer airlock hatch would not open. This impacted the plan to evaluate the EVA tools that would be used for the construction and maintenance of the International Space Station.

Upon return from the mission, troubleshooting revealed that the airlock actuator that is used for latching and unlatching the hatch was defective. This actuator was removed and replaced. Troubleshooting on the removed actuator revealed that a small screw had come loose from an internal assembly and lodged in the planetary gears of the actuator. Space Shuttle Program Corrective Action Record Number AE0959-010 documented this problem. The Failure/Problem Report Number NSLAD-RE-97-044 documented the actuator findings. Both of these reports are attached to this Lesson Learned input.
lesson:
The science of Human Spaceflight is a very non-forgiving process. In this case, a dislodged screw jammed a gear assembly thus preventing a hatch from opening during a space mission. This impacted the mission by preventing the EVAs from occurring. Something as simple as a small screw provided a major impact to the mission objectives. Attention to the details of installing the screws in the actuator gearbox and not noticing that there was no running torque provided the conditions where the screw fell out and jammed the actuator gear. Additionally, there was no simple way to screen for this failure. This hatch had successfully flown on a number of previous missions and had successfully passed the pre-flight functional check-out and closed nominally prior to launch, but then failed to operate properly during the mission.



STS-80 Actuator Gear Box Assembly with embedded screw in gears



STS-80 Actuator Gear Box Assembly showing missing and loose screws
recommendation: A uniform methodology for the installation of all fasteners should be provided early in the design phase of the program. This fastener specification should be imposed on all vendors/contractors responsible for hardware assemblies on the space vehicle. Where applicable, locking threads with running torques and final torques should be imposed on all assembly drawings. Additionally, the Shuttle Orbiter hatch actuators are essentially multi-geared torque multipliers containing numerous small parts which cannot be easily maintained. Despite several successful ground cycles of the hatch actuator, the problem was not identified until flight, and was not repairable in-flight. Future designed should give serious consideration to less elegant designs. Designs with less complexity, lower parts count, and the ability for in-flight maintenance, in-flight repair or in-flight work-around should be given a higher priority in design trade studies. It is easy to design something more complicated with added features and additional failure modes, but more difficult to build it to be simple and robust with fewer failure modes; future designers should strive for the latter.

title: Considerations for Helium Environments
driving_event:
The Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL) is a laser-based sensor capable of providing precision velocity and altitude relative to three laser-illuminated spots.  The NDL transmits three laser beams in fixed directions relative to each other.  Signals from each beam provide platform velocity and range to the ground along the laser line of sight.  Figure 1 shows a schematic of the NDL system. 

 

Figure 1. Diagram of the Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL)

The NDL failure on the Blue Origin New Shepherd NS-17 flight can be traced to a helium purge that occurred prior to launch.  The purge reduced the optical filter temperature, resulting in a filter center frequency shift.  The shift in the filter center frequency degraded the fiber amplifier input power, leading to a laser energization failure.  Without laser energization, the system could not collect the desired velocity and range data.

After the flight failure, controlled tests were performed to confirm the impacts of helium on the functioning of NDL.

When the optical filter was purged with helium, nitrogen, and air in separate test environments, different effects were seen on the optical filter.  Figure 2 shows the fiber amplifier input power in these different tests.  The top left plot shows what happened during the NS 17 flight.  The power decayed after the helium purge was initiated.  The lower left plot shows the fiber amplifier input power maintaining its nominal power during a nominal power-on and a power-on with a nitrogen purge introduced into a chamber containing the optical filter.  The top right plot shows different behavior after a helium purge is introduced into the chamber containing the optical filter.  Here, there is significant power decay.  Finally, the lower right plot contrasts the fiber amplifier input power with the filter located inside the chamber subjected to the helium purge (as in the top right plot) and with the optical filter located outside the chamber.  The only instance of a fiber amplifier power drop occurred when the optical filter was exposed to helium.  The tests demonstrate that it is the optical filter exposure to the helium purge that is responsible for the decay in the fiber amplifier power.

Figure 2. Fiber Amplifier input power under numerous conditions.

These issues were caused by helium’s ability to permeate into the cavity of the optical filter combined with the high thermal conductivity of helium relative to air.  When the helium purge occurred, helium was able to enter the optical filter cavity, greatly increasing the thermal conductivity of the resultant gas mixture in the cavity.  The increased thermal conductivity of the gas mixture enhanced the rate at which heat could be transferred from the optical filter, and exceeded the ability of the heaters to maintain the set temperature.  This result led to cooling in the optical filter and a subsequent shift in the filter center frequency, resulting in failed laser energization.

The NDL project was treated as a highly risk tolerant mission.  The higher risk tolerance led to certain concessions in terms of testing and analysis during the development and assembly, integration and test.  Exposure to helium was considered benign from a material compatibility perspective.  Thus, during instrument development, the optical filter was tested in both air and vacuum, but not in a helium environment.  Post-failure, elevated thermal conductivity representing the presence of helium was incorporated into the thermal analysis, and that analysis showed a possible reduction in average filter temperature sufficient to impact the bandpass frequency and produce a failure to energize.  However, testing was required to fully support the analysis.

Helium’s relatively small molecular diameter coupled with its chemical inertness enhances its ability to penetrate many seals.  In another helium-related failure, during the development of Hemispherical Resonator Gyroscopes (HRGs), a secondary vacuum cavity surrounding the primary cavity containing the HRG was added to bring the leak rate down to an acceptable level (David Rozelle, The Hemispherical Resonator Gyro: From Wineglass to the Planets, January 2009, Advances in the Astronautical Sciences 134:1157-1178).  Helium permeation appears to have also been the culprit in the immobilization of hospital employee iPhones in 2018 after a helium leak occurred in an Illinois Hospital (iPhones are Allergic to Helium, Kyle Wiens, October 30, 2018, IFIXIT; Helium temporarily bricks iPhones and Apple Watches in Chicago hospital, Android devices immune, Michael Potuck, October 31, 2018, 9TO5Mac).
lesson:
1. Helium has a higher thermal conductivity than air and therefore can affect the thermal stability of systems.  Testing in air and in vacuum does not envelope the thermal environment in which helium may be present.
  2. Helium’s small molecular size and chemical inertness enables it to permeate into instruments and devices exposed to helium.  Seals that are not specifically designed to prevent helium intrusion are susceptible.
recommendation:
• Helium has a higher thermal conductivity than air, this difference in thermal conductivity must be considered in system thermal analysis when applicable.
  • Special seals may be required to prevent helium permeation into susceptible devices.
  • If a mission exposes devices and/or instruments to helium, they should be screened and/or tested for helium susceptibilities.  Generally speaking, systems should be tested in environments they will see through all mission phases.  This recommendation goes hand in hand with NASA’s “Test as you fly, fly as you test” philosophy.

title: End-to-End Redundancy Analysis
driving_event:
The Launch Release Subsystem (LRS) is a critical electrical subsystem located on the Mobile Launcher (ML).  LRS generates the signals used to release and retract the umbilicals from the Space Launch System (SLS) vehicle at T-0/launch.  It is also used to command and monitor the Launch Abort System (LAS) and Booster Ignition Safe and Arm (S&A) devices as well as Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage (ICPS) functions. 

Due to the critical nature of most LRS functions, redundancy was heavily considered during the design and development phase; however, an issue with the redundancy architecture was identified after the subsystem already completed certification.  The root cause of the problem was that the redundancy and failure analysis for LRS was incomplete.  The analysis only reviewed how LRS interfaced with the end items (umbilical release mechanisms, S&A devices, etc) and did not consider potential failure scenarios of other subsystems that interface with LRS. 

During the design and development phase, a complete end-to-end evaluation/analysis of redundancy and potential failure scenarios should be performed.  The analysis should not be limited to only the subsystem under review but should also account for all interfacing subsystems.
lesson: Early in the design and development phase, a complete end-to-end analysis should be developed for signal paths to help identify potential failure scenarios that could eliminate end item redundancy.  The analysis should include all relevant interfacing subsystems (i.e. Ground Special Power, facility power, KGCS/comm, etc) and should not just be limited to the single subsystem and its associated signals under review.
recommendation:
• A visual tool such as a matrix/chart or end-to-end line diagram (ref Figure 1 and Figure 2) was found to be helpful in completing this assessment.   An example matrix can be seen in Table 1, which shows the LRS PLC assignments (second row) for each end item signal (left column) as well as the KGCS comm rack/gateway assignment for the PLC’s (top row).  It can easily be seen from such a layout that end items 1 through 3 have redundant LRS PLC’s, but both of the PLC’s would be lost if the 34612 comm rack or Gateway 1 were lost; therefore, visibility/control of end items 1 through 3 would also be lost. 

Table 1 – LRS End Item Signal Path Matrix for Baseline Architecture

  • Creation of line diagrams or matrices would enable identification of vulnerabilities in fault redundancy for each signal, and visualization of potential re-assignments of control/monitoring channels for corrections.

Table 2 - LRS End Item Signal Path Matrix for Updated Architecture

 

Table 2 shows the updated matrix after the LRS PLC A3 and B1 fiber connections were swapped.

title: Static Software Analysis of the NASA Autonomous Flight Termination Software
driving_event:
The NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) was requested by the Commercial Crew Program (CCP) Chief Engineer to identify deficiencies within certain AFTS CASS software builds. The AFTS CASS assessed was version 1.1 (CASS OR1 Update1), a very early release.

Note: The CASS developers improved the software development processes for the development of the CASS Operational Release 2 (OR2) release. The issues reported by the static code analysis of CASS OR1.1 have all been addressed in the CASS OR2 release. The static analysis tools verified complete adherence to Motor Industry Software Reliability Association (MISRA) C++ 2008 with no issues.
lesson:
The Lessons Learned from the Static Software Analysis of the NASA Autonomous Flight Termination Software (AFTS) were:

 

  • The definition of the software coding standards was non-specific. A general statement of “C++ is a suboptimal language for use in safety critical systems, deficiencies in the language are mitigated to an acceptable level by adherence to the MISRA C++ 2008 coding standard”. The “acceptable level” was never defined.
 
  • No procedures were documented in the software development plan regarding the configuration of the analysis tools, or the process of assessing the reported issues
recommendation:
Recommendations made at the conclusion of the NESC assessment involve updating sections of NPR 7150.2, “Software Engineering,” which pertain to software coding standards and software static analysis.

 

In general:

  • Software development teams should specify specific coding standards to be applied to the software development for both ground utilities and flight software.
  • Software development teams should configure the static analysis tool to best match the specified coding standard. Matching the coding standard and the static analysis tool capability leverages the tool as a verification asset.
  • Software development teams should define how the reported issues are to be reviewed, and what defines an issue that should be corrected.

title: AIAA/ANSI Standard S-120A-2015_R2019, Mass Properties Control for Space Systems, should be applied in context.
driving_event: The overarching purpose of the NESC PR Red Team was to evaluate and assess the mass management activities of the potential PR providers, assess the mass growth allowances (MGA) provided by the concept developers, and apply system and subsystem expertise to the proposed approaches, with an eye toward expected mass impacts of those design approaches. The team set out to use the S-120A MGA table and soon found gaps in the hardware categories. For instance, although the standard’s table cites “mechanisms” as a hardware category, and there are mechanisms on the rover, there is no reference information for the suspension and drive train required for a roving vehicle.
lesson: In the early stages of the NESC PR Red Team’s assessing PR mass management approaches, it became apparent that, although the S-120A MGA standard table provided a variety of ranges in a variety of typical space system hardware categories, it was important to use them only as a framework. The team developed additional hardware categories to address the suspension and drivetrain of a rover space system and used the “mechanisms” hardware category as a starting point. The application of system-specific experience required 1) the development of different categories and adjusted approaches for this specific space system application, and 2) the development of a tailored MGA table that took into account different hardware categories or systems from the typical designs for which S-120A is applied.
recommendation:
Space system developers should utilize the framework, concepts, and approaches outlined in S-120A and the recommended practices of SAWE RP A-3 as a guide, but tailor the MGA table for each system’s specific Concept of Operations and design.

 

 

Reference 

  1. International Society of Allied Weight Engineers (SAWE) RP A-3, Recommended Practice for Mass Properties Control for Space Systems. January 26, 2016.

title: TVAC Lamp Spectrum
driving_event:
The spectrum of the quartz lamps originally used for the Stratospheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment (SAGE) III on the International Space Station (ISS) Instrument Assembly (IA) Thermal VACuum (TVAC) testing did not match the assumed spectrum used in the thermal model.

To achieve correlation with the thermal model, a test was performed to characterize the solar flux level within the chamber as well as the chamber thermal gradients. This allowed for an improved correlation of the IA model; however, the additional time and resources required to perform the characterization test and complex model correlation were not ideal.

For the Instrument Payload (IP) TVAC test, a heater plate system was designed, built and installed in the facility. This system, coupled with the chamber’s cold shroud, provided the necessary environments for the IP to reach its temperature targets without using the quartz lamps.
lesson: Quartz lamps supply radiant heat largely in the solar spectrum, but the distribution depends upon lamp setting which creates significant complications for model correlation. Correlating results with a thermal model may be easier and more successful by using heater plates rather than developing a thermal model to account for the necessary details of the lamp spectrum.
recommendation: If it is desired to correlate thermal models to TVAC test data, it is best to avoid the use of quartz lamps.

It focuses on those lessons that should have the greatest significance to the Directorate during the formulation of program and mission plans. View the attached report.
